<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-clean-rm-81560dec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ff1ba1637aad6e3">Why distinguish two preference-flip rates rather than estimate one overall error rate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aclean-rm">CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>True positives flipped negative and true negatives flipped positive can have different causes. Estimating each conditional rate corrects observed-label risks separately; one error rate hides asymmetry.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A length-biased annotator may reject correct short answers at a different rate than they accept incorrect long answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.21138-clean-rm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ff1ba1637aad6e3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:clean-rm" data-paper-title="CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5aea70a8fd94cd32">Why match semantics as well as recovered preference, and may negative risk be clipped?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aclean-rm">CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matching preference proportions alone can align semantically unrelated examples. Joint optimal transport uses representation distances and recovered preferences to estimate both noise rates. Fixed corrected loss can be negative; clipping changes its expectation, and inaccurate rates also break unbiasedness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two domains can have half positive labels while one flips them often; use semantic representations to expose the difference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.21138-clean-rm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5aea70a8fd94cd32">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:clean-rm" data-paper-title="CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b0ba45f5b5fa7573">How does freezing the CleanRM noise estimator differ from jointly updating it with the reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aclean-rm">CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A frozen estimator defines a fixed corrected risk. Joint updates move its coefficients and can lower loss by changing the explanation of noise. This is a different objective without the same fixed-rate risk interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Estimate label flips before training; don&#x27;t reinterpret temporarily misclassified samples as noisier.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.21138-clean-rm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b0ba45f5b5fa7573">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:clean-rm" data-paper-title="CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4642fc40ad22ddae">Should CleanRM clamp recovered labels or corrected losses to their conventional ranges?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aclean-rm">CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Recovered preferences can fall outside [0,1] and corrected risks are signed. Clamping changes the debiasing objective. Require rates summing to less than one and freeze the estimator during RM updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A valid negative corrected loss should not be reset to zero for prettier curves.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21138v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.21138-clean-rm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4642fc40ad22ddae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-gaw-po-bf9dde22" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7bb97a727465c23f">Does GAW-PO label complete replies or each token as preferred/rejected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Labels compare two replies to one prompt; there is no per-token annotation. Rejected replies can contain good steps or shared wording. Gradient alignment supplies credit at a finer granularity, not additional human token truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both answers start with the correct equation and differ only at the end, the rejection does not label the shared equation wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7bb97a727465c23f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0307c820f34c8286">Why penalize rejected-response tokens less if they support the preferred direction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A whole response&#x27;s rejection does not condemn all tokens. Smaller negative weights for aligned gradients avoid suppressing shared useful steps. This changes credit, not factual verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both openings are right and only the rejected conclusion is wrong, an aligned opening needn&#x27;t receive the same penalty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0307c820f34c8286">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-013be2268305c60d">How does GAW-PO gradient alignment differ from weighting by token likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Likelihood measures how often the current model produces a token. Alignment measures whether penalizing it conflicts with preferred updates. Common tokens can be irrelevant and rare tokens helpful; this is a mechanism comparison, not an empirical ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not punish a rare term merely for low probability if it supports a correct explanation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-013be2268305c60d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:gaw-po" data-paper-title="GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-92390bc26a92b79e">How does GAW-PO&#x27;s positive-part cosine handle aligned, orthogonal and opposite gradients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agaw-po">GAW-PO: Preference Optimization with Gradient-Aligned Token Weights</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight is one minus positive cosine. Perfect alignment approaches zero; orthogonal/opposite directions keep weight one; partial positive alignment reduces penalty. Actual gradients are required. Local evidence is only the weight kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A negative cosine is first set to zero, so the weight does not exceed one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01511">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2610.01511-gaw-po/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92390bc26a92b79e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:compo" data-paper-title="A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-compo-257a1fd8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-65f82773739e80be">Does COMPO&#x27;s black-box optimization change prompts instead of weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acompo">A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It updates model parameters without backpropagating through the preference objective. It needs parameter perturbation and an objective comparator. Prompt-only remote access does not satisfy that requirement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Load and compare two nearby checkpoints; editing chat prompts is another search.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19144">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.19144-compo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-65f82773739e80be">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:compo" data-paper-title="A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e824d210b2c1f79">How does COMPO infer a direction from paired perturbations, and why threshold it?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acompo">A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Which of positive and negative perturbations performs better on the same objective gives a directional sign. One-bit feedback is noisy, so coordinate thresholds suppress unreliable components. Objective sampling and evaluation still cost resources.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare small forward/backward perturbations under fixed preferences; leave unreliable coordinates unchanged.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19144">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.19144-compo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e824d210b2c1f79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:compo" data-paper-title="A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-76db661a1119217d">What information do COMPO&#x27;s zeroth-order comparisons and first-order backpropagation need?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acompo">A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>First order needs a differentiable objective and backward access; zeroth order ranks perturbed evaluations. Repeated comparisons still cost compute and noise affects direction; no backward pass does not imply free or more accurate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A preference judge can rank two variants without returning gradients for any layer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19144">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.19144-compo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-76db661a1119217d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:compo" data-paper-title="A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-318c54c96ba1d744">Why threshold each coordinate after a COMPO one-bit update?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Acompo">A Zeroth-Order Paradigm for LLM Preference Alignment</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Berkeley</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One comparison gives coarse information and weak coordinates may reflect noise. Thresholding suppresses them but can remove small genuine signals. Local tests cover comparison oracle and threshold kernel, not LLM alignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A coordinate consistently near zero may be suppressed, not automatically deemed useless.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19144">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.19144-compo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-318c54c96ba1d744">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sd-dpo" data-paper-title="Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sd-dpo-8723680d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4cc0854feb5b0998">Does Style-Debiased DPO update knowledge or enforce one writing style?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asd-dpo">Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Waseda University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Synthetic preferences should update knowledge; stylistic differences are confounders. Concision or ornament is not factual truth. That distinction motivates factual checks and group balancing rather than stylistic personalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same knowledge may be expressed in a sentence or a paragraph; both should stay correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与实现对应. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16532">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.16532-sd-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4cc0854feb5b0998">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sd-dpo" data-paper-title="Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dc95882a3e62042c">Why reverse a preference if the rejected answer is factual?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asd-dpo">Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Waseda University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Synthetic preferences can mislabel stylistic differences as knowledge errors, causing ordinary DPO to suppress correct expressions. Identify those replies and reverse their preferences with group-ratio weights to cancel style gradients. Reliable factual assessment and grouping are prerequisites.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If both replies are factual but one is more courteous, directly following the label may teach courtesy rather than knowledge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与实现对应. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16532">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.16532-sd-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dc95882a3e62042c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sd-dpo" data-paper-title="Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1ee0ad22878bbd9">How does SD-DPO reversal differ from dropping stylistic pairs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asd-dpo">Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Waseda University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Dropping removes their contribution. Reversing with group-proportion weighting seeks to cancel an existing style direction. Factual correctness must be assessed first, or reversal could promote wrong answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Check both formal and colloquial variants for correctness before balancing their style signals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与实现对应. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16532">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.16532-sd-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1ee0ad22878bbd9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sd-dpo" data-paper-title="Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b16448413bb6fd49">Do local SD-DPO factual scores establish that a real judge recognizes truth?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asd-dpo">Style-Debiased DPO: Updating LLM Knowledge with Factuality-Aware Synthetic Preference Data</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Waseda University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Fixed inputs supply the scores. The code tests reversal and group-balanced loss under given labels, not automated factual judging or knowledge gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the test declares an answer factual, correct reversal validates the rule, not identification of the fact.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与实现对应. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16532">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2609.16532-sd-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b16448413bb6fd49">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-normalized-dpo-59718764" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d8f5f2448d0d1fc9">Is Normalized DPO&#x27;s margin a human score gap or a model-relative preference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is the model-side value in the loss. Data identify the winner; policy and reference probabilities determine the margin and beta sets its scale in the preference curve. Normalization does not rewrite labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A human says A beats B without saying by three points; current probabilities still give a margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d8f5f2448d0d1fc9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6f9a407550fa6eb6">Why can dividing by beta change gradients without moving Normalized DPO&#x27;s optimum?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>At fixed positive beta, subtracting a constant and multiplying by a positive scalar preserve optima. Ordinary DPO couples preference-curve scale with update size; dividing centered softplus by beta removes an extra beta in the margin gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reducing beta can weaken ordinary updates; normalization separates curve scale from step-size effects.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6f9a407550fa6eb6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e56aa9d911938bb">Is Normalized DPO equivalent to changing the learning rate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Centering and dividing by beta rescales loss gradients. Learning rate scales the optimizer&#x27;s update. They can be related under simple conditions, but momentum/adaptive statistics can change the trajectory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A second-moment optimizer need not maintain identical state under external step-size and loss scaling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0e56aa9d911938bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:normalized-dpo" data-paper-title="Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c8ea679e776c4425">How can normalized DPO avoid zero-over-zero for tiny beta?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Anormalized-dpo">Disentangling Optimization Scale from Preference Scale in DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Affiliation not listed in the paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compute centered softplus minus log 2 stably or use its small-beta limit. The gradient is negative sigmoid and does not vanish from an extra beta factor. Test the limit rather than substituting zero in the quotient. Candidate checks are not full training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Confirm finite limiting loss and gradient instead of catching exceptions and returning zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.27032-normalized-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c8ea679e776c4425">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grip" data-paper-title="GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-grip-70305ebb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3564cca28d3e1319">Does GRIP produce one merged model or run thinking and instruct models on every request?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrip">GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It interpolates corresponding aligned parameters into one model and runs that model. It does not select experts online or generate two answers and vote. Arbitrary architectures cannot be combined without matching weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Combine same-shape layer weights before one forward pass, not two responses followed by length selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25583">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.25583-grip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3564cca28d3e1319">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grip" data-paper-title="GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-043e5c5450e52cbc">Why learn fine-grained interpolation instead of one ratio for thinking and instruct weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrip">GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Layers and parameters serve different capabilities, so a uniform mix can weaken reasoning and brevity. Reward-guided coefficients vary across weights. The local probability interpolation is a proxy, not the paper&#x27;s weight-combination validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Preserve computation habits while reducing redundant explanation by using different coefficients across parameter regions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25583">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.25583-grip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-043e5c5450e52cbc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grip" data-paper-title="GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9c01e1412413fd6">How does GRIP interpolation differ from lowering inference temperature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrip">GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight interpolation changes distributions across contexts. Temperature rescales existing logits for one forward pass. Both can change length without representing the same mechanism or combining learned capabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Merging can change the favored reasoning step; lower temperature generally emphasizes already higher logits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25583">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.25583-grip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9c01e1412413fd6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:grip" data-paper-title="GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1dad8a09f9c6a8fb">What shape and evaluation constraints apply to GRIP interpolation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agrip">GRIP: Granular Reward-Guided Parameter Interpolation for Efficient Reasoning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Peking University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight tensors and coefficients must align at the stated granularity; broadcasting must match layer or parameter semantics. Rewards must follow the allowed data protocol. A deterministic candidate diagnostic does not prove paper-checkpoint reasoning or length gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not broadcast layer coefficients as vocabulary-column coefficients merely because multiplication works.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25583">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.25583-grip/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1dad8a09f9c6a8fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-pto-55a5beae" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ab711475e2acf5fb">What do PTO&#x27;s dialogue policy, virtual user and oracle do, and which is updated?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The policy proposes replies, the virtual user continues possible interactions, and the oracle evaluates expanded branches. Their comparisons label preferences for the current state and update only the dialogue policy. Simulated users and evaluators provide training signals, not real user behavior or joint updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A consultation agent asks two possible questions, the simulator answers each, and the oracle compares progress. Train the agent&#x27;s current reply selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ab711475e2acf5fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ba4418ae346a8ba2">Why simulate later dialogue before labeling a current PTO response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pleasing immediate reply may harm long-term goals. Compare rolled-out user interactions and turn branch-level differences into current-response DPO preferences. Depth changes cost and horizon; simulator/oracle bias becomes training bias and is not real feedback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guessing a need can read better in turn one, while simulating another turn may show clarification prevents a wrong direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ba4418ae346a8ba2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ade76e34fb07aaaa">What does adding more PTO branches expand compared with looking farther ahead?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Width compares more actions at one state; depth observes consequences farther into the future. Both cost simulations and judgments but aren&#x27;t substitutes. Shallow branches can miss delayed effects; one deep branch can miss better starts. This is a search distinction, not an empirical ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Five openings with one turn each increase width; one opening with many turns increases depth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ade76e34fb07aaaa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:pto" data-paper-title="Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a3b00a1932c6dec">Why preserve the mapping from current histories to future PTO branches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Apto">Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Reichman University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One preference pair compares actions from the same state. Continue each action in its own branch and do not leak future outcomes into policy inputs. Deterministic local evaluators replace the expensive oracle only to test tree and credit flow.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If A prompts clarification and B confusion, attaching A&#x27;s success to B reverses the preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12062-pto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a3b00a1932c6dec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-c2-dpo-2993ea41" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-24a30e0257152972">Why does C²-DPO require a response pair and two contexts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Chosen/rejected compare responses to the same prompt; complete/degraded context varies evidence. They are independent axes. Hold the responses fixed to isolate context&#x27;s effect.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare red car and blue car with the original and degraded images, not with different questions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-24a30e0257152972">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-35469067fe68386f">Why compare full and degraded context margins rather than only raise chosen likelihood?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Chosen likelihood may exploit language priors and ignore images. Context preference gain rewards the same pair changing preference with evidence while preserving the original ordering. It depends on appropriate degradation and does not itself establish correct visual understanding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If masking a chart leaves preference unchanged, language priors may dominate; correct evidence should provide extra support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-35469067fe68386f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb62ba4316cf25a3">Is positive context preference gain the same as the chosen response winning under full context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. CPG compares the two margins; winning needs a positive full-context margin. An improved but negative margin can still favor the wrong reply. Context gain and original preference ordering are separate constraints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A change from −3 to −1 gives positive gain without a chosen win.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb62ba4316cf25a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:c2-dpo" data-paper-title="Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-86d4bee16225c912">What must stay consistent across C²-DPO&#x27;s margins?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Ac2-dpo">Context Blindness in DPO: Mitigating Object Hallucination in MLLMs via Context-Calibrated Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Korea University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use one prompt and one chosen/rejected pair under both contexts. Degraded context must not contain the answer. Local work does not complete fine-tuning the named multimodal model/data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Subtracting a full-image A/B comparison from degraded-image C/D does not isolate visual evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12158">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2608.12158-c2-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86d4bee16225c912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rm-memorization-protocol" data-paper-title="What do Reward Models Memorize?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rm-memorization-protocol-fc530cbb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-18ac1f819b98e581">Why separate in-training and held-out performance in reward-model memorization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arm-memorization-protocol">What do Reward Models Memorize?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ILLC, University of Amsterdam</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A high score on a seen pair could reflect broad learning or memorization. Compare the same pair across actual runs including and excluding it; the difference measures conditional memorization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare models trained with this pair to models that did not see it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24484v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.24484-rm-memorization-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-18ac1f819b98e581">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rm-memorization-protocol" data-paper-title="What do Reward Models Memorize?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-13c11fab85e1d0ae">Why sigmoid each reward margin before averaging by inclusion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arm-memorization-protocol">What do Reward Models Memorize?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ILLC, University of Amsterdam</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sigmoid is nonlinear. Convert each actual run&#x27;s margin into a probability, then separately average seen and held-out runs for memorization and generalization. Their difference can be negative. Group by actual manifests and keep users isolated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Large margin differences can be hidden by averaging before probability saturation; retain each run&#x27;s membership.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24484v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.24484-rm-memorization-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-13c11fab85e1d0ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rm-memorization-protocol" data-paper-title="What do Reward Models Memorize?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-cb91206f6cb57754">How does CM differ from training accuracy minus test accuracy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arm-memorization-protocol">What do Reward Models Memorize?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ILLC, University of Amsterdam</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>CM compares the same pair across runs and splits by user to avoid leakage. Aggregate split means also mix difficulty differences. CM depends on split and training quality; it is not proof of verbatim memorization per item.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A train–test gap between different user groups may reflect their difficulty rather than memory of any one preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24484v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.24484-rm-memorization-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cb91206f6cb57754">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rm-memorization-protocol" data-paper-title="What do Reward Models Memorize?" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b6cbf37a01cc1dc1">Can inclusion in reward-model training be inferred from a high score?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arm-memorization-protocol">What do Reward Models Memorize?</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ILLC, University of Amsterdam</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use actual run manifests to assign inclusion and held-out status; scores are outcomes. Inferring inclusion from outcomes is circular. Check user-level isolation. The local aggregator does not create the paper&#x27;s training runs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high-scoring held-out pair stays held out; do not move it to support a memorization story.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24484v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2607.24484-rm-memorization-protocol/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b6cbf37a01cc1dc1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-dpo" data-paper-title="Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-sa-dpo-319b4acc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5b5098de671ca213">Does SA-DPO measure semantic distance between responses or between prompts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-dpo">Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research / Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It compares preferred and dispreferred answers to one prompt. It is not a margin from prompt difficulty/length. Frozen response representations supply semantic distances independently of preference labels; distances aren&#x27;t correctness scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two paraphrases of one answer can be close; two similar prompts are not the comparison unit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27733v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.27733-sa-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5b5098de671ca213">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-dpo" data-paper-title="Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-006c8557a58ba088">Why require less separation for semantically similar answers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-dpo">Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research / Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A large fixed margin spends capacity separating paraphrases and amplifies label noise. SA-DPO scales the added margin with frozen semantic distance, zero at zero distance, while keeping relative-to-reference preference. Control encoder quality and mean pressure separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>&#x27;The answer is three&#x27; and &#x27;The result is 3&#x27; need less separation than right vs wrong answers; wording can still bias distances.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27733v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.27733-sa-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-006c8557a58ba088">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-dpo" data-paper-title="Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b5ab87cfeaf71fbf">Why match mean margin when comparing SA-DPO to a fixed-margin method?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-dpo">Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research / Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Otherwise performance can change from overall training pressure rather than semantic allocation. Matching means better isolates allocation without proving semantic judgments always correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An easier objective from a smaller mean margin does not establish better semantics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27733v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.27733-sa-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b5ab87cfeaf71fbf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:sa-dpo" data-paper-title="Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b5a27901e7c2d8b2">What should SA-DPO do when response distance is zero?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asa-dpo">Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research / Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Set extra distance margin to zero, but retain the policy/reference log-ratio difference in preference loss. Use frozen distances, not constants or test-label calibration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Removing extra separation for identical wording does not make the whole loss zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27733v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.27733-sa-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b5a27901e7c2d8b2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-group-dpo-93d61191" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b8740cc2992f39de">Does GroupDPO concatenate all responses into one long response?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. One prompt has nonempty positive and negative sets; responses retain separate probabilities and IDs. The joint objective uses set relationships without requiring simultaneous activation storage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two positive and two negative answers are encoded independently while the objective compares both sets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b8740cc2992f39de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-31c1d45cb19d9504">Why not recompute GroupDPO coefficients inside each response microbatch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze derivatives from the entire group at the same parameter point and replay response gradients to recover the first-order result. Local recomputation changes sets and normalization. Recompute after every update. Loss values and Hessians are not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Each response carries fixed full-group credit rather than re-ranking within a small compute batch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31c1d45cb19d9504">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ee0899295d4a06f6">Are GroupDPO Margin, MPO, Softmax and All-Pairs equivalent objectives?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. They compare sets differently. What is shared is precomputing derivatives of the chosen full-group objective and replaying separately. Changing the objective differs from changing compute batches while retaining its first derivative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>All pairwise comparisons may assign different coefficients than pooling positives first; the same memory method serves both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ee0899295d4a06f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:group-dpo" data-paper-title="GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
