<h2 id="qa-c09b70ec0aa149ab">Can GroupDPO coefficients be reused after the optimizer step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Agroup-dpo">GroupDPO: Memory-Efficient Group-Wise Direct Preference Optimization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Derivatives change with parameters. Recompute. Do not divide microbatch backpropagation by local groups or microbatch count; positive NLL also uses the full-batch group normalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reusing old coefficients saves a pass but becomes a stale approximation, not exact current gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15602v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2604.15602-group-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c09b70ec0aa149ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-probabilistic-autorater-421e42ad" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-86cdf4efbe8d3fa3">Why should a probabilistic autorater output a preference probability, not just a winner?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Real preferences can disagree. Brier/log rewards fit observed preference frequencies rather than force binary certainty. Reliable target distributions matter; arbitrary numbers are not calibrated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near-even annotator votes warrant an intermediate probability rather than an absolute winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-86cdf4efbe8d3fa3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f08ba902f4cd5432">Why can&#x27;t Autorater backpropagate through parsed probability text?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The policy generates text, parses it to a fixed reward and uses policy gradients. Discrete text-to-float parsing has no ordinary differentiable path. Brier/log rewards encourage calibration, with separate invalid penalties. Derivatives of numeric scores alone are not GRPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unformatted &#x27;very confident&#x27; response fails parsing; don&#x27;t silently substitute a plausible number.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f08ba902f4cd5432">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-87f7465105cb6097">How do Brier and log rewards penalize confident errors differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both are proper probability scores, but squared and logarithmic tails differ; log loss is especially sensitive to extremely confident mistakes. Parse failures also have a separate reward, beyond legal probability gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A near-certain win prediction followed by defeat is penalized by both, with different magnitudes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-87f7465105cb6097">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:probabilistic-autorater" data-paper-title="Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-37c219be1787c9bd">Why can&#x27;t invalid numbers enter the formula before multiplying by a zero mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aprobabilistic-autorater">Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate invalid outputs first. NaN can propagate through nonlinearities and multiplication by zero; out-of-range values are not probabilities. Use the parse-failure reward. The local strict parser is a contract, not the authors&#x27; parser or full RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Route NaN directly to invalid reward rather than computing log(NaN) first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00263v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2510.00263-probabilistic-autorater/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37c219be1787c9bd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-benchmark-self-bias-143e8f64" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7ea7ef39b1edfe7d">Which axis is target, which is benchmark role, and which cell measures self-evaluation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The target is evaluated; the benchmark role performs evaluation. Self-evaluation is the diagonal where they match. Compare own and other roles for one fixed target, not different targets.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A answering with B judging is off-diagonal; A answering and judging is diagonal. Keep A as the target in both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7ea7ef39b1edfe7d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bae0503700524a2d">Why rank each segment and exclude self from the peer mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Segment scales may differ, so rank before averaging to preserve the protocol. Remove self from the peer comparison. Score direction, axes and tie handling affect the sign; peer consensus is not external truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A low-is-better metric and high-is-better metric need consistent rank direction. Never put the self score back into peers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bae0503700524a2d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b2350803a5a27539">How does the protocol distinguish self-evaluation advantage from a stronger model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compare one target&#x27;s ranks under its own role and peers to isolate evaluator preference from target quality. Peers can share biases, so this is relative audit evidence, not a definitive capability verdict.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Consistently leading under all judges differs from leading only under one&#x27;s own judge.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b2350803a5a27539">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:benchmark-self-bias" data-paper-title="When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0b238a5ebb648838">Why do axis order and leave-self-out matter for self-bias?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Abenchmark-self-bias">When LLMs Benchmark Themselves: Deconstructing Self-Bias in Automated Evaluation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank within segments, average over segments, then subtract the peer mean excluding self from the diagonal. Specify whether scores are higher- or lower-is-better; negative bias indicates favorable self-rank.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>MetricX-QE is lower-is-better. Descending ranks would reverse the bias direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26600v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2509.26600-benchmark-self-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0b238a5ebb648838">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-simpo-d55ff0e4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-19268f541c6ed5d9">Does reference-free SimPO mean there is no training feedback?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Chosen/rejected pairs still supply preferences. It removes a resident reference model, using length-averaged policy log-probability as implicit reward with a fixed margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>You still need a better answer label; no frozen reference scores need be computed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-19268f541c6ed5d9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-864ca18fd75dda04">Without a reference, how does SimPO avoid favoring short responses by sequence probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Total log probability accumulates per token and changes reward scale with length. Average per token and require the preferred response to beat the rejected one by a margin, without an extra reference forward. This removes one length effect, not all quality bias.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A short wrong answer can beat a longer correct one on summed log probability; averaging removes the direct sum-length penalty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-864ca18fd75dda04">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-85c5fbdd0f8ee884">Is SimPO&#x27;s training margin equivalent to reducing inference temperature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Margin sets desired average-reward separation and changes parameter gradients. Temperature rescales next-token logits at inference. They can coexist but shorter output at one temperature does not validate the margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Training compares complete response average log probabilities; inference temperature doesn&#x27;t read that preference pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-85c5fbdd0f8ee884">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:simpo" data-paper-title="SimPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cb729e6cab9ed41b">Which tokens enter SimPO&#x27;s log-probability sum and length?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asimpo">SimPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use the same valid-response mask for both; no padding or prompt tokens. The loss updates only the policy. A token objective does not reproduce the paper&#x27;s judge/model matrix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Counting padding in the denominator distorts the short answer&#x27;s average reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2405.14734-simpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cb729e6cab9ed41b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-orpo-e4a32db7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-898ddc81df5c3d9b">What is the difference between ORPO odds and probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Probability p is an event&#x27;s share of all outcomes. Odds p/(1−p) compare occurrence to nonoccurrence and can exceed one. ORPO compares preferred and rejected odds, not percentages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>p=1/2 gives odds 1; p=3/4 gives odds 3, not 300% probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-898ddc81df5c3d9b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-713377bce48ffbf5">What do SFT and the odds-ratio term each constrain in ORPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT raises chosen likelihood; the odds term widens separation from rejection. Both update one policy without reference in the objective. Odds are boundary-sensitive. Reporting reference KL as a diagnostic does not add it to training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Raising only chosen likelihood can also raise similar bad answers; odds explicitly separate them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-713377bce48ffbf5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b37223053c895c4">How does ORPO&#x27;s single stage differ from SFT followed by separate preference optimization?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One policy update combines chosen NLL and preference odds without a resident frozen reference for another stage. Two-stage training first produces an SFT policy then changes objective/reference. One stage is not universally better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One preference batch supplies NLL and odds gradients instead of finishing chosen-only SFT first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b37223053c895c4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:orpo" data-paper-title="ORPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-533c71e635c7676c">Why handle probabilities near zero or one in ORPO&#x27;s log-odds margin?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aorpo">ORPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · KAIST</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Log odds are log(p)−log(1−p), then contrasted across replies. Boundaries cause log zero or huge ratios. The local kernel adds 1e−12 to both terms and uses logaddexp, not probability subtraction. Candidate probabilities are not token-level response probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>0.9→0.99 is +0.09 probability but odds go 9→99.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2403.07691-orpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-533c71e635c7676c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-kto-edf0a49a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea3586d73fba657b">Are KTO desirable and undesirable weights feedback probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Labels describe single accepted/rejected outputs; λ weights control class utility contributions. Class frequency and explicit weight are separate, neither a predicted satisfaction probability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rebalance many upvotes and few downvotes without inventing matched same-question pairs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea3586d73fba657b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2aa2521a67232958">How does KTO update from single desirable feedback without same-prompt pairs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use response policy/reference log ratio against expected KL as a dynamic baseline and define separate desirable/undesirable utilities. Independent examples can be reweighted without fictitious comparisons. Reference and imbalance still matter; a label is not absolute reward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Upvote and downvote on separate inquiries enter separate branches, not a fabricated preference pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2aa2521a67232958">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7b11de358098425">Does KTO differ from DPO only by unpairing the data?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. KTO defines gains/losses around a KL reference point; DPO compares same-prompt response margins. Standalone feedback cannot be arbitrarily paired, and class weights alter tradeoffs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One user&#x27;s upvote and another&#x27;s downvote on different queries do not order their answers to one prompt.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7b11de358098425">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:kto" data-paper-title="KTO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-51338639a8b4c3b6">What is KTO&#x27;s reference point, and what does the local policy establish?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Akto">KTO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Contextual AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is expected policy-to-reference KL, not one answer&#x27;s log ratio. Separate aggregate baseline and sample signal. The local six-candidate linear policy checks this relation, not free generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compare a high log ratio to the moving baseline; don&#x27;t treat the example as the entire KL expectation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2402.01306-kto/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-51338639a8b4c3b6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-self-rewarding-38dd38b1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b295099775e750b6">Does a Self-Rewarding judge tie reveal the preferred answer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A tie gives no strict preference; display order cannot create one. Candidate count and distinguishable judging are separate. Even unequal scores are the current judge&#x27;s judgment, not new human truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two candidates tie, don&#x27;t label the first shown the winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b295099775e750b6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-154b2587d78b6046">Where do Self-Rewarding LM preferences come from, and why can errors compound?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each round ranks its own generated candidates and trains the next round with DPO on those judgments. They are not independent human labels; persistent judge biases can become stronger. Keep external held-out evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A judge rewarding verbosity may repeatedly choose long arithmetic errors; an external check can break the loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-154b2587d78b6046">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-64e85cc5effd028f">How does Self-Rewarding differ from a fixed external reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed judge doesn&#x27;t coevolve; self-reward hopes both generation and judgment improve but can amplify shared errors. Compare at equal budget with independent evaluation, not rising self-scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A model can learn to please its own scoring rule without becoming more useful to users.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64e85cc5effd028f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:self-rewarding" data-paper-title="Self-Rewarding LM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7824f1f8ceec3d9a">What provenance must Self-Rewarding iterations retain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aself-rewarding">Self-Rewarding LM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Record generating policy round, judge round and pair-selection rule. Don&#x27;t backfill old data with post-update scores. Use isolated evaluation. Local tests cover state and objective, not paper judge quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After training a new model, don&#x27;t rescore old candidates and present those scores as original supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.10020-self-rewarding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7824f1f8ceec3d9a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-spin-6b40abc1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-2d79d9ecff10c497">Where do SPIN positives come from without new human preference data?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Existing human SFT demonstrations stay positive. The previous policy generates negatives on the same prompts. Self-play changes negatives and reference; it still uses demonstrations and generated replies are not necessarily factually wrong.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A standard answer already exists; generate a comparison without asking a human to rank it again.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2d79d9ecff10c497">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0b13386310cfbca">How does SPIN&#x27;s previous-policy negative differ from self-judged preferences?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Human demonstrations are positives; prior-policy samples are negatives. Train relative to the prior policy, then refresh it. No self-judge scoring is needed. Human supervision remains and negatives aren&#x27;t necessarily false.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use fixed expert examples and regenerate opponents next round instead of replaying all old negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0b13386310cfbca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-de51d109d380cea3">How does SPIN&#x27;s refreshed negatives differ from repeated SFT on fixed examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>SFT raises fixed demonstration likelihood. SPIN resamples a comparison distribution from the previous policy on the same prompts and distinguishes demonstrations from it. Both negatives and relative reference change, not just training rounds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After fixing earlier mistakes, the next opponent may make different ones. Fixed SFT won&#x27;t refresh those negatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-de51d109d380cea3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:spin" data-paper-title="SPIN" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-68b65f63205056ef">Why freeze SPIN&#x27;s opponent during a round and refresh it afterward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aspin">SPIN</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of California, Los Angeles</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The previous policy supplies both samples and the reference. Changing it mid-round changes the objective. Refresh after the round to align generation, scoring and updates. No full-scale local text experiment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Using old reference for half the batches and a new one for the rest does not define one consistent round.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2401.01335-spin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68b65f63205056ef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ipo" data-paper-title="IPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-ipo-127b83ec" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3ab275343c2f6b76">Does increasing τ increase or decrease IPO&#x27;s target gap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aipo">IPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The finite target is 1/(2τ), so increasing positive τ decreases the gap. It is not a label-strength score; training outcomes also depend on data, policy and optimization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Changing τ from 1 to 2 changes 1/2 to 1/4; this is formula arithmetic.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.12036-ipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3ab275343c2f6b76">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ipo" data-paper-title="IPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-27d91eff39b627ea">Why fit a finite IPO gap rather than always separating chosen and rejected farther?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aipo">IPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Logistic losses can keep enlarging a separable margin, risking overfit. IPO squares error to a finite reference-relative log-ratio target. Overshooting reverses the gradient. This changes loss shape, not just learning rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Once separation is sufficient, continued suppression of rejection need not help; excess separation is corrected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.12036-ipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-27d91eff39b627ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ipo" data-paper-title="IPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c593b9604bc999a9">Does fitting IPO&#x27;s gap require the chosen response&#x27;s absolute probability to increase?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aipo">IPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The gap is chosen-minus-rejected policy/reference log ratios. Raising chosen, lowering rejected or both can reach the target. Chosen probability alone omits the relative comparison and global normalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Chosen can stay fixed while rejected falls and the gap grows.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.12036-ipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c593b9604bc999a9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:ipo" data-paper-title="IPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-90a4386f929b6180">Why use a cross policy/reference probability ratio in IPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aipo">IPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It measures how much the preferred-over-rejected relationship changed relative to reference, not just policy probability difference. Use a fixed positive τ and target 1/(2τ), aggregate response tokens correctly and retain reference terms.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If reference already favors a wording, the cross-ratio distinguishes inherited preference from added change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.12036-ipo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-90a4386f929b6180">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:steerlm" data-paper-title="SteerLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-steerlm-863fe2af" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8618eab53654c787">Are SteerLM&#x27;s attribute predictor and conditioned generator the same role?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asteerlm">SteerLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The predictor annotates existing answers with helpfulness, quality and other dimensions. The generator learns to produce answers under target attributes supplied at inference; it does not need a future answer scored first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Annotate training replies as concise/helpful, then request new replies conditioned on those attributes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05344">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.05344-steerlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8618eab53654c787">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:steerlm" data-paper-title="SteerLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a8ee45efddccf43">Why condition generation on attributes instead of aggregating all rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asteerlm">SteerLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A single scalar makes preference mixtures hard to change at inference. Predict attributes, then train conditional SFT so users can specify combinations. Labels must be reliable, and control does not guarantee precise independent satisfaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ask for detailed but restrained or concise and friendly without retraining a policy for each combination.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05344">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.05344-steerlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a8ee45efddccf43">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:steerlm" data-paper-title="SteerLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6818c23101e01b24">How does SteerLM differ from asking for brevity in an inference prompt?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asteerlm">SteerLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attribute-conditioned SFT systematically associates labeled values with response patterns. A one-off natural-language instruction needn&#x27;t have that training signal. They can coexist, but adding attribute text alone is not conditioned training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Training examples across concision levels give an inference level learned meaning beyond wording.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05344">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.05344-steerlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6818c23101e01b24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:steerlm" data-paper-title="SteerLM" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d29a44f99cbc4fc3">Are local SteerLM attribute labels equivalent to the authors&#x27; predictor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Asteerlm">SteerLM</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Deterministic reward axes on public candidates supply local labels to test the interface. No large attribute predictor or free-text conditioned generator is trained. Preserve attribute order and value domains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Swapping quality and length columns may run while reversing user controls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05344">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2310.05344-steerlm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d29a44f99cbc4fc3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlaif" data-paper-title="RLAIF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-rlaif-a542b4bc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-04d1061c5a5f15e4">Which human work does RLAIF replace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlaif">RLAIF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>AI compares candidate preferences to reduce pairwise human labeling and supplies strategy training signals. Evaluation criteria and independent assessment remain. AI labels can have position, style and knowledge biases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>People can specify criteria while AI compares summaries; its scores aren&#x27;t objective truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00267">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2309.00267-rlaif/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-04d1061c5a5f15e4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlaif" data-paper-title="RLAIF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dfd8d3776378be1d">Why swap candidate order for RLAIF judging, and can raw scores be averaged?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlaif">RLAIF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Judges may favor earlier positions. Evaluate both orders and combine only after mapping to the same candidate identity. Raw positional averaging can cancel a true preference. It controls position, not factual, style or value biases.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Convert both trials to A&#x27;s win score before averaging.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00267">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2309.00267-rlaif/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dfd8d3776378be1d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlaif" data-paper-title="RLAIF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0cc21caa8f68e6b2">How does RLAIF training differ from an AI choosing an answer at inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlaif">RLAIF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training converts judgments to data and updates parameters. Inference selection changes one response without learning. Similar judges may be used, but costs and effects on future requests differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Selecting a reply today changes today&#x27;s output; training on the pair may change tomorrow&#x27;s policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00267">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2309.00267-rlaif/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0cc21caa8f68e6b2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:rlaif" data-paper-title="RLAIF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e9950599cb9a6017">How does local RLAIF keep identities straight when swapping order?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Arlaif">RLAIF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Map each judgment back to original candidate IDs before combining labels. Fixed labels verify mapping and update, not a full judge or large RL.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If left wins on pass two and B is now left, credit B rather than A.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00267">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2309.00267-rlaif/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e9950599cb9a6017">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-dpo-0073c0b6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5b1bca6549e89038">Why doesn&#x27;t DPO need a separately fitted reward model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The KL-regularized policy expresses implicit reward as a policy/reference log ratio. Direct paired classification uses chosen and rejected labels. Reward information still comes from preference supervision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With labels on two answers, compute the paired loss without first training a scorer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5b1bca6549e89038">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f795703a61b6c34c">Why use DPO policy changes relative to reference instead of raw answer probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw scores inherit pretraining preferences. Relative ratios measure redistribution against the baseline, jointly comparing preferred/rejected in the classification margin implied by KL regularization. No explicit reward model, but same-prompt preferences and fixed reference remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If a phrase starts with high likelihood, distinguish inherited preference from a further supervised increase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f795703a61b6c34c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb674fbd601d1a3d">How does DPO&#x27;s data flow differ from reward-model PPO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Classic DPO consumes fixed preference pairs without sampling and reward-model scoring at every step. PPO usually includes those stages. A fixed dataset may omit states future policies visit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A preference bank without a wrong-prefix category doesn&#x27;t automatically gain it from offline updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb674fbd601d1a3d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:dpo" data-paper-title="DPO" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d9471cd43ba2d2a4">Why freeze DPO&#x27;s reference and align response masks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Adpo">DPO</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Stanford University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The reference anchors changes; updating it changes the objective. Score identical response tokens in both paths, with neither prompt nor padding mismatches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Adding prompt likelihood only to reference introduces irrelevant input length into the margin.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.18290-dpo/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d9471cd43ba2d2a4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<span id="paper-post-training-slic-hf-5def3201" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c231dcb6386ca8e">Why combine sequence calibration and supervised loss in SLiC-HF?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ranking makes preferred likelihood exceed rejected likelihood. Supervision learns trusted content rather than succeeding only by suppressing bad replies. Both train the generator directly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separate good from bad summaries while learning the good summary itself.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c231dcb6386ca8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fc913597b1af1378">Why keep supervised cross-entropy when SLiC-HF already has a preference margin?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=post-training%3Aslic-hf">SLiC-HF</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relative ranking does not prevent overall language drift. Cross-entropy preserves reference response likelihood, combining calibration and generation learning. Off-policy data do not remove coverage, length or source differences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Suppressing bad answers can satisfy ranking even while good answers get worse; supervision retains good generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10425">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../post-training/2305.10425-slic-hf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fc913597b1af1378">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="post-training:slic-hf" data-paper-title="SLiC-HF" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="post-training" data-theme="post-training" data-topic="post-training/preference-and-alignment">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">LLM post-training / Preference and alignment: identify the feedback first</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
